input.question: Would a suction cup still have the ability to stick to a surface in a vacuum?
input.ground_truth: When a suction cup is pressed against a surface, it pushes out all of the air beneath it and creates a vacuum between the cup and the surface. This vacuum holds the suction cup tightly, and it will continue to do so until the pressure on the outside of the cup becomes lower than the pressure on the inside of the cup. (from [ehow](_URL_0_)) In a vacuum, the pressure outside will be the same as the pressure outside, so no, it will not stick to a surface.

Okay! Imagine you have a toy that sticks to the wall because it has a sticky circle, like a suction cup.

Now, if you go into space where there is no air (that’s called a vacuum), the suction cup might not stick the same way. On Earth, the suction cup works because the air around it gets pushed out when you press it on something, and the air outside pushes it back.

But in space, where there is no air, when you press the suction cup, the air can’t go anywhere. So, there’s nothing to push the cup back onto the wall. That’s why the suction cup might not stick in a vacuum.

So, the answer is: No, a suction cup probably won’t stick in a vacuum because there is no air to help it stick.
